DUBAI, United Arab Emirates (CNN) -- The United Arab Emirates has refused to grant a visa to a female Israeli tennis player, preventing her from competing in the Sony Ericsson World Tennis Association Tour in Dubai, the WTA said in a statement Sunday. The UAE has refused to grant a visa allowing Shahar Peer to compete in Dubai. Shahar Peer would have been the first Israeli athlete to participate in a professional sporting event in the UAE, CNN Sports correspondent Pedro Pinto said. The UAE has no diplomatic ties with Israel. Peer told CNN on Sunday evening she was "very, very disappointed" to be denied access to the tournament. "Any player that qualifies should attend, and I was prevented," she said from Israel. "I'm glad the WTA support me. A red line was crossed for every athlete in the world -- politics should be kept separate from sports." The governing body of women's tennis said it was "deeply disappointed" that Peer was being denied entry to the country hosting the tournament, but it did not cancel the competition, which began Sunday. The move runs counter to WTA policy, which says no player should be barred from competing in a tournament for which she has qualified. Dubai could lose its membership in the WTA tour next year over the ban on Peer, according to WTA rules. That would mean professional players could compete only in exhibition matches in Dubai, the results of which would not count in pro rankings. Government officials in Dubai have not responded to CNN's request to comment over their refusal to allow Peer to compete in the event. "Ms. Peer has earned the right to play in the tournament, and it is regrettable that the UAE is denying her this right," said Larry Scott, chairman and chief executive of the tour.  Watch Scott express disappointment » . "Following various consultations, the tour has decided to allow the tournament to continue to be played this week, pending further review by the tour's board of directors." The patron of the Dubai Tennis Championships is Dubai's ruler, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al-Makhtoum. Two million dollars in prize money is on the line. Al-Makhtoum told CNN in 2004 that Dubai would accept Israeli students to a school dedicated to students from the Middle East who are talented at sports. In 2003, Dubai hosted World Bank and International Monetary Fund meetings, which Israeli government officials attended. The Israeli flag -- among other member states' flags -- is still part of a globe monument in Dubai. Peer, 21, is ranked 48th in the world among female tennis players. She was allowed to compete at the Doha tournament in Qatar last year, where she received a warm welcome, according to Israeli daily newspaper Haaretz. Qatar, another Gulf Arab state, froze diplomatic ties with Israel after Israel's military offensive in Gaza last month. Peer downplayed the political undertones of her participation in last year's Doha tournament, telling Haaretz that she didn't come to Qatar "to help the politics of course." But she added that if her playing in the tournament "can help for peace or anything, I'd be really happy." Scott said the tour will "review appropriate remedies for Ms. Peer" as well as "appropriate future actions with regard to the future of the Dubai tournament." Peer was advised Saturday by tournament and WTA officials of the denial of her visa while she was participating in a tournament in Pattaya, Thailand, according to a WTA statement. The Dubai Tennis Championships runs through February 28.

Scott said the WTA would consider suitable remedies for Peer and determine what further measures might be taken concerning the future of the Dubai event.

A WTA statement said tournament and tour officials informed Peer on Saturday that her visa had been denied. At the time, she was playing in another tournament in Pattaya, Thailand.

# UAE Bars Israeli Tennis Star Shahar Pe’er From Dubai Tournament

**February 16, 2009 — DUBAI, United Arab Emirates**

The United Arab Emirates has prevented Israeli tennis player Shahar Pe’er from competing in this week’s Dubai Tennis Championships by denying her an entry visa, despite her qualification for the elite professional event.

Pe’er, then ranked among the world’s leading women’s players, had been scheduled to compete in the Women’s Tennis Association tournament beginning Monday. Tournament officials confirmed that she could not enter the country after UAE authorities refused to issue the necessary visa.

The decision has triggered sharp criticism from the WTA, international media organizations and advocates of keeping political disputes out of professional sport.

“Ms. Pe’er has earned the right to play in this tournament,” WTA chief executive Larry Scott said in a statement. The tour said it was reviewing the circumstances surrounding the visa denial and warned that the incident could affect Dubai’s standing as a host of major tennis events.

Pe’er called the exclusion disappointing but said she would not allow it to derail her career.

“I have played tournaments all over the world, and I believe sport should bring people together,” she said in comments reported after the decision became public. “I am very disappointed that I was not given the opportunity to compete.”

## Organizers cite circumstances beyond their control

The Dubai Tennis Championships said it had sought a visa for Pe’er but was informed that she would not be admitted. Organizers stressed that immigration decisions are made by the UAE government, not by tournament officials.

Officials also cited concerns about potential protests following Israel’s recent military offensive in the Gaza Strip. The conflict, which ended with ceasefires in January, generated widespread anger across the Arab world.

Tournament representatives suggested that Pe’er’s appearance could have provoked demonstrations and raised security concerns. Critics rejected that explanation, arguing that organizers of an international competition are responsible for ensuring that every qualified athlete can participate safely and on equal terms.

The UAE does not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel and generally does not admit travelers carrying Israeli passports, although exceptions have occasionally been made for international sporting and diplomatic events.

## WTA faces pressure to respond

The visa denial presents a serious challenge for the WTA, which sanctions the lucrative Dubai tournament and requires events to provide equal access to eligible players.

The Dubai competition is among the most prominent stops on the women’s tour, offering substantial prize money and attracting many of the world’s highest-ranked players. Pe’er’s exclusion raises questions about whether tournaments should be awarded to countries that may deny entry to athletes because of nationality.

Scott said the WTA had learned of the final decision too late to relocate or cancel the tournament without severely affecting the players and the tour calendar. Nevertheless, he indicated that sanctions against the event were possible.

“We will review appropriate remedies for Ms. Pe’er and also review the future of the Dubai tournament,” he said.

The tour is expected to consider financial penalties, compensation for Pe’er and guarantees that qualified players will be admitted in future years.

## Television network cancels coverage

The Tennis Channel, a U.S.-based cable network, announced that it would not televise the tournament in protest.

Network chairman and chief executive Ken Solomon said the decision to deny Pe’er a visa was inconsistent with the principles of international sport.

“Sport should be above politics,” Solomon said. “By preventing a player from competing solely because of her nationality, the organizers have undermined the integrity of the event.”

The Wall Street Journal’s European edition also reportedly withdrew its sponsorship from the tournament, increasing commercial pressure on organizers and the WTA.

## Wider implications for international sport

Pe’er, who has represented Israel in the Olympics and the Fed Cup, has previously competed in Muslim-majority countries under heightened security. Her case is likely to intensify debate over the responsibilities of nations hosting international sporting events.

Tennis authorities generally require tournament hosts to admit all qualified competitors regardless of nationality, religion or political disputes. The Olympic movement follows a similar principle, though athletes from countries without diplomatic relations have repeatedly faced visa problems, boycotts or refusals to compete against one another.

The controversy may also affect the men’s Dubai Tennis Championships, scheduled to begin next week. Israeli players entered in that event could face the same immigration restrictions, while other competitors may come under pressure to withdraw in solidarity with Pe’er.

For now, the women’s tournament is proceeding without her. But the dispute has shifted attention away from the court and toward a broader question confronting global sport: whether a country can host a major international competition while excluding an otherwise eligible athlete because of the passport she carries.
